case_analysis.focal_point: Whether plaintiffs who win only a preliminary injunction—and then have their case mooted by subsequent legislative repeal—qualify as a “prevailing party” entitled to attorneys’ fees under 42 U.S.C. § 1988.
case_analysis.legal_provision: 42 U.S.C. § 1988(b) (“prevailing party” attorneys’ fees in certain civil rights actions, including suits under 42 U.S.C. § 1983).
case_analysis.petitioner_position: Petitioner (Virginia DMV Commissioner) argues that a party is not a “prevailing party” under § 1988 unless it obtains (1) a conclusive merits determination in its favor (not merely a preliminary, predictive likelihood-of-success finding) and (2) an enduring, judicially ordered change in the parties’ legal relationship. A preliminary injunction granted under the Winter standard is provisional and subject to revision; if the case later becomes moot because the legislature repeals the challenged law, the ultimate change is attributable to a non-judicial event rather than a final judicial resolution. Allowing fees in this posture would effectively revive a “catalyst” theory (fees triggered by voluntary change rather than judicial relief) and would overextend fee shifting to cases that never reach a definitive merits judgment.
case_analysis.respondent_position: Respondents (plaintiffs challenging the license-suspension statute) argue that they are “prevailing parties” because the district court entered an enforceable preliminary injunction that carried judicial imprimatur and materially altered the legal relationship by prohibiting enforcement of the challenged statute against them, delivering concrete, court-ordered relief. They contend that § 1988 does not invariably require a final merits judgment if the court order provides meaningful merits-based relief, and that mootness caused by later legislation should not erase prevailing-party status when plaintiffs already obtained binding judicial relief that directly benefited them.
key_precedents: Winter v. Natural Resources Defense Council, Inc. (preliminary-injunction standard; likelihood of success)
Sole v. Wyner (preliminary injunction later undone; not prevailing)
Lefemine v. Wideman (judicial order materially altering legal relationship; prevailing-party principles)
Buckhannon Board & Care Home, Inc. v. West Virginia Department of Health & Human Resources (rejecting catalyst theory; requires judicial imprimatur)
Smyth v. Rivero (Fourth Circuit; preliminary injunction generally insufficient for prevailing-party status)

John Roberts.reasoning: Justice Jackson’s concern that denying fees would invite strategic mooting after plaintiffs secure an enforceable preliminary injunction is the strongest equitable point on the other side, but § 1988’s term-of-art “prevailing party” as construed in Buckhannon and Sole v. Wyner still requires a court-attributable, durable alteration that reflects entitlement—not merely interim, predictive relief under Winter that is later overtaken by legislative repeal. Justice Sotomayor is right that the injunction had judicial imprimatur and real effect while in force, yet tying fee eligibility to that temporary period would necessarily reintroduce catalyst-style disputes about whether (and how much) the injunction “caused” repeal, shifting fees from judicial resolution to nonjudicial change. Lefemine, as Justice Jackson invokes it, does not undermine this because it involved permanent, merits-linked relief that conclusively fixed the parties’ rights, unlike a stand-alone preliminary injunction followed by mootness without a final merits disposition or consent decree. A narrow, administrable holding—no prevailing-party status when the only judicial relief is a preliminary injunction and the case becomes moot due to legislative repeal—best preserves our precedents and institutional legitimacy.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor’s fairness concern—that plaintiffs should not lose fees after securing enforceable, court-ordered interim protection—does not overcome the term-of-art limitation in § 1988(b) to a “prevailing party” as Buckhannon defines it: an enduring, court-attributable alteration of the parties’ legal relationship. A Winter preliminary injunction is expressly provisional and revisable, and when the case ends in mootness by legislative repeal, the only lasting change is nonjudicial, so awarding fees would functionally reintroduce the catalyst theory Buckhannon rejected. Justice Jackson’s reliance on Lefemine does not undermine that conclusion because Lefemine involved operative, permanent injunctive relief that finally resolved entitlement, not stand-alone interim relief that never ripened into a merits judgment or consent decree. Sole v. Wyner’s central insight—that preliminary success unmoored from an ultimate, merits-linked judicial resolution is too “ephemeral” to confer prevailing-party status—applies with full force here.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: Justice Jackson’s strongest point is that an enforceable preliminary injunction is judicially sanctioned relief that materially alters the parties’ legal relationship while it lasts, so fees would be tethered to a court order rather than mere voluntary change. But Buckhannon’s term-of-art “prevailing party” requires a court-attributable, merits-based alteration with sufficient durability, and Winter makes clear a preliminary injunction is predictive and revisable rather than a conclusive adjudication of entitlement. As the Chief Justice and Justice Kagan stress, once the case is mooted by legislative repeal, any enduring change is attributable to the legislature, and awarding fees here would in practice reintroduce catalyst-theory causation inquiries that Buckhannon rejected. Lefemine does not undermine this conclusion because it involved final, operative relief on the merits, not stand-alone interim relief that never ripened into a definitive judicial resolution.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: Chief Justice Roberts’s administrability and “enduring, merits-based” framing does not, to my mind, answer the decisive point that the plaintiffs obtained a court-ordered, enforceable preliminary injunction that actually barred the government from enforcing the challenged law against them for a meaningful period—this is judicially sanctioned relief, not mere catalyst-theory happenstance. Justice Kagan and Justice Alito rely heavily on Sole v. Wyner’s “ephemeral” language, but that case involved interim relief that was later undone by an adverse merits judgment; here there was no merits loss and no vacatur or reversal, so mootness-by-repeal should not retroactively nullify the legal alteration the court itself imposed. Winter’s provisional framework, emphasized by Justice Thomas, speaks to the standard for granting interim relief, not to whether such relief—once granted and complied with under threat of contempt—can “materially alter” the parties’ legal relationship for § 1988 purposes while it is operative. Denying fees in this posture would, in practical effect, encourage strategic mooting after plaintiffs have secured real court-ordered protection, undermining § 1988’s remedial function for civil-rights enforcement and access to justice.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor and Justice Jackson make the best point that a preliminary injunction is judicially sanctioned and enforceable while it lasts, so it is not a purely extra-judicial “catalyst.” But under Buckhannon and Sole v. Wyner, “prevailing party” is a term of art tied to relief that durably and conclusively alters the parties’ legal relationship in a way attributable to the court; a Winter preliminary injunction is expressly predictive and revisable, and mootness by legislative repeal means the only lasting change is nonjudicial. Justice Jackson’s invocation of Lefemine does not undermine that framework because Lefemine involved permanent (or effectively final) injunctive relief that resolved entitlement, whereas here there is no final merits disposition or equivalent decree to anchor fees. I also share Chief Justice Roberts’s administrability concern: recognizing fees here would pressure courts to litigate causation and strategic mooting in a manner that functionally reintroduces the catalyst theory Buckhannon rejected.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor and Justice Jackson fairly emphasize that a preliminary injunction is judicially enforceable and thus not mere private settlement or voluntary change. But under Buckhannon, “prevailing party” is a term of art requiring a judicially sanctioned alteration with the durability of a merits disposition (or consent decree), and Winter underscores that preliminary injunctions are predictive and revisable rather than adjudications of entitlement. Sole v. Wyner’s warning about “ephemeral” interlocutory wins applies with equal force where the case becomes moot by legislative repeal, because the only enduring change is nonjudicial; awarding fees would effectively revive the catalyst theory by tying fee eligibility to whether interim relief was followed by repeal. Justice Jackson’s invocation of Lefemine does not undermine this analysis because that case involved permanent, operative injunctive relief that conclusively altered the parties’ rights, unlike a stand-alone preliminary order that never ripened into final judicial relief.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor’s best point is that a preliminary injunction is judicially enforceable and undeniably alters the parties’ relationship while in effect, so mootness should not “erase” what the court did. But Buckhannon’s term-of-art “prevailing party” requirement, as the Chief Justice stresses, is keyed to an enduring, court-attributable change akin to a merits judgment or consent decree; when repeal moots the case, the only permanent alteration comes from the legislature, not the judiciary. Sole v. Wyner’s emphasis on the “ephemeral” nature of interim relief, reinforced by Winter’s expressly predictive, revisable framework, counsels against treating a stand-alone preliminary injunction as the functional equivalent of final relief—otherwise we invite backdoor catalyst-theory litigation over whether interim success “caused” repeal. Justice Jackson’s concern about strategic mooting is a policy consideration, but it cannot override the administrable, precedent-based line our cases draw between provisional relief and conclusive judicial resolution.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor and Justice Jackson press the hardest point: the preliminary injunction was enforceable and carried judicial imprimatur, so it materially altered the parties’ relationship while it lasted and mootness should not erase that reality. But under Buckhannon the operative term of art is a court-attributable, enduring alteration of the parties’ legal relationship, and as the Chief Justice and Justice Kagan emphasize, tying fees to interim relief that becomes moot through legislative repeal risks collapsing back into catalyst-theory causation disputes about whether the injunction “prompted” the change. Sole v. Wyner’s “ephemeral” rationale applies not only when interim relief is later undone on the merits, but more broadly where the court never issues a conclusive, merits-based resolution establishing entitlement to relief; Winter confirms the preliminary-injunction posture is predictive and revisable rather than adjudicative in the requisite sense. Lefemine does not alter my analysis because, as Justice Roberts notes, it involved operative, permanent injunctive relief that conclusively settled rights, whereas here the only lasting change is nonjudicial repeal.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: Chief Justice Roberts’s administrability concern—that fees here would backdoor Buckhannon’s catalyst theory by making entitlement turn on whether repeal followed interim relief—has force, but it misdescribes the causal anchor: the fee request is tethered to a court-issued, enforceable injunction that altered the parties’ legal relationship while it operated, not to the legislature’s later choice. Justice Kagan’s reliance on Sole v. Wyner is the closest precedent, yet Sole’s “ephemeral” point rests on interim relief being overtaken by an adverse merits determination; mootness by repeal does not repudiate the court’s earlier legal judgment or erase the concrete protection the order provided. Winter’s “predictive” nature of preliminary injunctions goes to the strength of the merits showing, not to whether the order is judicially sanctioned and enforceable—§ 1988’s practical function is served by recognizing prevailing status where plaintiffs secured actual court-ordered restraint and the case ends without any reversal or vacatur. On my pragmatic view, the Petitioners’ rule would systematically encourage strategic mooting after plaintiffs have already won meaningful, court-ordered protection, undermining civil-rights enforcement and procedural fairness.

John Roberts.reasoning: Section 1988’s “prevailing party” requirement, as construed in Buckhannon, demands judicially sanctioned, merits-based relief that materially alters the parties’ legal relationship in a way attributable to the court, not merely a party’s later voluntary change. A preliminary injunction issued under Winter is provisional and predictive, and Sole v. Wyner teaches that such interim relief—when not followed by an enduring merits resolution—does not suffice for prevailing-party status. Where the case becomes moot because the legislature repeals the challenged law, the ultimate, permanent change is not “court-ordered” in the Buckhannon sense, and awarding fees risks recreating the catalyst theory. A narrow rule denying fees in this posture best respects precedent and avoids expanding fee liability based on nonfinal, revisable injunctions.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: Section 1988(b) authorizes fees only for a “prevailing party,” a term of art that, as Buckhannon explains, requires a judicially sanctioned, enduring alteration of the parties’ legal relationship—typically a judgment on the merits or consent decree—not merely a temporary interlocutory order. A preliminary injunction under Winter rests on a predictive likelihood-of-success determination and is inherently provisional and revisable, so it does not conclusively establish entitlement to relief. When the case becomes moot because the legislature repeals the challenged law, any lasting change is attributable to nonjudicial action, and awarding fees would effectively resurrect the catalyst theory Buckhannon rejected. Sole v. Wyner confirms that preliminary-injunction success, without ultimate merits victory, does not make a plaintiff a “prevailing party” under § 1988.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: Section 1988(b)’s term “prevailing party” is best read, consistent with Buckhannon, to require a judicially sanctioned, merits-based alteration of the parties’ legal relationship that is not merely provisional and that is attributable to the court rather than to subsequent legislative change. A preliminary injunction under Winter rests on a predictive “likelihood of success” and is inherently tentative and revisable; when the case becomes moot due to repeal, any enduring change is produced by the legislature, not a final judicial resolution, risking an end-run around Buckhannon’s rejection of catalyst-theory fee awards. Sole v. Wyner confirms that preliminary, non-final relief that does not culminate in a conclusive merits determination cannot confer prevailing-party status, and extending fees here would invite substantial fee exposure based on temporary orders that may never be tested on the merits. The Fourth Circuit’s approach in Smyth v. Rivero is therefore more faithful to § 1988’s text and this Court’s prevailing-party jurisprudence.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: Section 1988’s “prevailing party” inquiry turns on whether the plaintiff obtained judicially sanctioned, enforceable relief that materially altered the parties’ legal relationship, not on an inflexible requirement of a final merits judgment. Here, the preliminary injunction carried the court’s imprimatur and provided concrete, court-ordered protection against enforcement, satisfying Buckhannon’s requirement of judicial relief rather than mere voluntary change. Sole v. Wyner denies fees when interim relief is later undone by an adverse merits judgment as “ephemeral,” but it expressly left open whether preliminary-injunction success can suffice absent a final merits loss, and mootness by legislative repeal does not retroactively erase the binding effect and real-world benefit of the injunction while it was in force. Denying fees in this posture would undercut § 1988’s remedial purpose by disincentivizing civil-rights challenges—often brought by vulnerable plaintiffs—where defendants can moot cases through legislative change after plaintiffs have already secured meaningful judicial protection.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: Section 1988(b)’s term “prevailing party” is a term of art requiring a judicially sanctioned, merits-based, and enduring alteration of the parties’ legal relationship, not merely interim relief. Under Buckhannon, fees cannot rest on a nonjudicial “catalyst” like subsequent legislative repeal, and a preliminary injunction—entered on a prediction of likely success under Winter—typically “does not resolve the merits” or supply the kind of conclusive relief that supports prevailing-party status. Sole v. Wyner reinforces that a plaintiff who secures only preliminary relief without a final merits judgment is not a prevailing party, especially where the suit ends without any judgment that the defendant violated federal law. Because the ultimate disposition here was mootness after repeal (not a merits judgment or consent decree), awarding fees would stretch § 1988 beyond its coherent, workable limits and invite catalyst-theory litigation.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: Section 1988(b)’s term “prevailing party” is a term of art that, as Buckhannon explains, requires a judicially sanctioned, material alteration of the parties’ legal relationship—typically through an enforceable judgment on the merits or a court-ordered consent decree, not merely interim, predictive relief. A preliminary injunction issued under Winter reflects only a likelihood-of-success assessment and is inherently provisional; when the case becomes moot due to legislative repeal, the lasting change is attributable to a nonjudicial act rather than an enduring judicial disposition. Sole v. Wyner confirms that preliminary relief that does not culminate in a final merits victory does not confer prevailing-party status. Treating a mooted preliminary injunction as sufficient would effectively revive the rejected “catalyst theory” and dilute § 1988’s plain meaning limits on fee shifting.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: Under 42 U.S.C. § 1988(b), a “prevailing party” must obtain a judicially sanctioned, enduring alteration in the parties’ legal relationship, not merely interim relief that rests on a predictive “likelihood of success” assessment under Winter. Sole v. Wyner teaches that a preliminary injunction, when not followed by a conclusive merits judgment in the plaintiff’s favor, ordinarily does not confer prevailing-party status; here, legislative repeal mooted the case before any final merits determination. Awarding fees in these circumstances would risk reintroducing the Buckhannon-rejected “catalyst theory,” because the lasting change is attributable to a non-judicial legislative act rather than a final court-ordered resolution. A clear rule denying fees for standalone preliminary injunctions also promotes administrability and respects judicial restraint by avoiding fee litigation untethered to final merits relief.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: Section 1988(b) authorizes fees only to a “prevailing party,” which this Court has read to require a court-ordered, enduring change in the parties’ legal relationship—not merely a transient shift in bargaining position. Under Buckhannon, a plaintiff does not prevail based on nonjudicial developments, and when the case becomes moot because the legislature repeals the challenged law, the lasting change is attributable to that repeal rather than to a final judicial resolution. Sole v. Wyner holds that a preliminary injunction that does not culminate in enduring relief cannot confer prevailing-party status, and Winter underscores the provisional, predictive nature of preliminary-injunction findings. Awarding fees here would stretch “prevailing” beyond its ordinary meaning and risk reintroducing the catalyst theory Buckhannon rejected.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: Section 1988(b) authorizes fees for a “prevailing party,” and under Buckhannon a plaintiff prevails when it obtains relief with judicial imprimatur that materially alters the parties’ legal relationship—here, an enforceable preliminary injunction barring enforcement of the statute against plaintiffs. Sole v. Wyner forecloses fees when interim relief is later undone by an adverse merits determination (“win the battle, lose the war”), but it does not squarely control where the preliminary injunction is never vacated or reversed and the case becomes moot due to legislative repeal. Given the practical consequences and fairness concerns animating § 1988, denying fees after plaintiffs secured concrete, court-ordered protection would undermine civil-rights enforcement and allow governments to moot cases post-injunction to evade fee liability. Lefemine reinforces that the touchstone is whether a court order provided real, operative relief changing the legal relationship, which this injunction did notwithstanding later mootness.

case_analysis.focal_point: Whether plaintiffs who obtained only a preliminary injunction before their case became moot can be treated as a "prevailing party" entitled to attorney’s fees under § 1988.
case_analysis.legal_provision: 42 U.S.C. § 1988(b) (fee-shifting for the "prevailing party" in certain civil-rights actions, including 42 U.S.C. § 1983).
case_analysis.petitioner_position: Petitioner (Virginia DMV Commissioner) argues that a preliminary injunction that merely reflects a court’s prediction of likely success—and that never culminates in a final, merits-resolving judgment because the case is later mooted by legislative repeal—does not confer "prevailing party" status. In petitioner’s view, § 1988 requires (1) a conclusive merits determination in the plaintiff’s favor, not a provisional likelihood-of-success assessment, and (2) an enduring, judicially caused alteration of the parties’ legal relationship; when the lasting change comes from a non-judicial event (the legislature repealing the challenged law), fees are not available.
case_analysis.respondent_position: Respondents (driver’s-license-suspension challengers) contend that the preliminary injunction was an enforceable court order carrying the necessary judicial imprimatur and was merits-based under the governing standard, materially altering the parties’ relationship by halting enforcement of the statute against them. They argue that obtaining that injunction provided concrete, court-ordered relief and thus makes them prevailing parties even though the case later became moot due to repeal, because they achieved the practical and legal benefit sought while the injunction was in force.
key_precedents: Winter v. Natural Resources Defense Council, Inc.
Buckhannon Board & Care Home, Inc. v. West Virginia Department of Health & Human Resources

John Roberts.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor and Justice Jackson press the strongest point: a preliminary injunction is judicially sanctioned, enforceable relief, and Sole v. Wyner reserved the mootness scenario—so a categorical rule would be overbroad. But Buckhannon’s administrable line still requires an enduring, merits-linked judicial alteration at the litigation’s resolution; a Winter-based likelihood-of-success order that dissolves through mootness, with the only lasting change coming from legislative repeal, risks functionally restoring the catalyst theory Buckhannon rejected. Justice Jackson’s reliance on Lefemine does not undermine that distinction because Lefemine involved final, merits-based injunctive relief, not provisional relief that never ripens into a conclusive entitlement. Consistent with judicial minimalism, the narrowest holding is that this kind of preliminary injunction, followed by mootness due to legislative repeal and no merits judgment or equivalent final relief, does not confer prevailing-party status under § 1988.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor’s best point is that a preliminary injunction is judicially sanctioned and enforceable, and Sole v. Wyner reserved the mootness scenario; but under the original legal meaning of “prevailing party,” as operationalized in Buckhannon, the plaintiff must obtain a judgment-like, merits-resolving disposition that endures as the case’s resolution, not provisional relief that dissolves with mootness. Winter underscores why: a preliminary injunction rests on a predictive “likelihood of success” assessment and does not conclusively establish entitlement, so treating it as “prevailing” untethers fees from final judicial relief and effectively revives the catalyst theory where the only durable change is legislative repeal. Justice Jackson’s invocation of Lefemine does not alter this analysis because that case involved final, lasting injunctive relief on the merits—precisely the kind of enduring court-ordered change absent here. As the Chief Justice notes, the administrable line Buckhannon draws tracks the text’s settled usage and avoids fee entitlement turning on interim orders and post-injunction legislative responses rather than conclusive judicial relief.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor is right that a preliminary injunction is judicially sanctioned and enforceable, and Sole v. Wyner reserved the precise mootness scenario, but that does not answer Buckhannon’s central requirement of a merits-linked, enduring alteration that defines who “prevailed” in the litigation. As the Chief Justice emphasizes, Winter injunctions are predictive and provisional; treating them as sufficient whenever the case later becomes moot risks converting fee eligibility into a backward-looking assessment of whether interim relief plus subsequent nonjudicial change (here, legislative repeal) “worked,” which is functionally the catalyst theory Buckhannon rejected. Justice Jackson’s reliance on Lefemine strengthens the point that final injunctive relief confers prevailing status, but it cuts against extending that label to interim relief that never ripens into a final, enforceable merits disposition. On a textual and administrable view, the only durable change here came from the legislature, not from a conclusive court-ordered remedy at the end of the case, so fees are unavailable.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: Chief Justice Roberts’ administrability concern—that fees should turn on an “enduring” alteration at the litigation’s conclusion to avoid a Buckhannon-like catalyst rule—has force, but it misdescribes what happened here: the plaintiffs obtained a judicially sanctioned, enforceable injunction that actually changed the parties’ obligations while it was in effect, not merely a voluntary policy shift. Justice Kagan’s proposed narrow exception (“effectively merits-final” preliminary relief) points in the right direction, and on my view Winter’s merits-inflected likelihood-of-success determination plus concrete, operative relief fits that exception when mootness prevents any subsequent merits reversal. Sole v. Wyner does not control because it addresses preliminary success followed by a merits loss; as Justice Jackson notes, it expressly left open the mootness scenario, and refusing fees categorically would invite governments to moot after being enjoined, undermining § 1988’s access-to-justice purpose for plaintiffs who need urgent protection. Lefemine reinforces that injunctions—when they deliver the requested practical relief with judicial imprimatur—can confer prevailing status, and the fact that the legislature later repealed does not erase the court-ordered change that occurred during the case.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor’s strongest point—that an enforceable preliminary injunction carries judicial imprimatur and gives real relief, and that Sole v. Wyner reserved the mootness scenario—does not, for me, overcome Buckhannon’s insistence that “prevailing” be tied to an enduring, merits-linked judicial alteration as the litigation’s resolution. A Winter-based preliminary injunction is typically predictive and provisional; when the case becomes moot through legislative repeal, the only lasting change is nonjudicial, and awarding fees risks functionally reviving the catalyst theory Buckhannon rejected. Justice Jackson’s reliance on Lefemine helps only where the injunction is final merits relief; it doesn’t translate cleanly to interim relief that never ripens into a conclusive merits disposition. I would keep the narrow possibility open (as the Chief Justice and I have noted) for the unusual case where the preliminary injunction is effectively merits-final and grants all the relief sought, but this record looks like the ordinary provisional order that shouldn’t suffice for § 1988 fees.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor’s best point is that a preliminary injunction is enforceable and bears judicial imprimatur, and Sole reserved the mootness posture; Justice Jackson similarly presses that Winter’s merits-inflected standard can supply more than a purely procedural win. But under Buckhannon’s textual understanding of “prevailing party,” the plaintiff must secure an enduring, merits-linked judicial disposition that resolves the case (or its functional equivalent), not a provisional likelihood-of-success order that dissolves when the legislature repeals the challenged law. Treating interim relief plus subsequent mootness as sufficient would, as the Chief Justice and Justice Kagan emphasize, effectively reintroduce a catalyst theory by tying fees to nonjudicial change rather than a conclusive court-ordered entitlement. Lefemine does not alter that conclusion because it involved lasting injunctive relief as the merits outcome, not a temporary order that never ripened into final, enforceable merits relief.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor’s strongest point is that a preliminary injunction is judicially sanctioned and enforceable, and Sole v. Wyner expressly reserved the mootness scenario—so this is not the pure “voluntary change” problem Buckhannon targeted. But Buckhannon’s administrable, legitimacy-preserving line (as the Chief Justice emphasizes) ties “prevailing party” to an enduring, merits-linked judicial disposition at the litigation’s end; a Winter-based likelihood-of-success injunction that dissolves by mootness does not supply a lasting court-ordered alteration, and the only durable change here is legislative repeal. Justice Jackson’s reliance on Lefemine doesn’t undermine that conclusion because Lefemine involved final, merits-based injunctive relief, whereas this case never produced a conclusive merits judgment or its functional equivalent. Awarding fees whenever interim relief precedes mootness would, in practical effect, recreate a catalyst regime and invite satellite fee litigation over provisional rulings—an outcome our precedent and institutional interests counsel against.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor’s best point is that a preliminary injunction has judicial imprimatur and is enforceable while it lasts, and Sole v. Wyner reserved the mootness scenario. But under the ordinary legal meaning of “prevailing party” as we applied it in Buckhannon, the plaintiff must secure an enduring, court-ordered alteration that resolves the claim or is equivalent to a final merits disposition; a Winter-style likelihood-of-success injunction that dissolves through mootness does not confer that kind of lasting entitlement. Justice Jackson’s reliance on Lefemine does not overcome this distinction because Lefemine involved final, merits-based injunctive relief, whereas here the only durable change is legislative repeal—making fees depend on a nonjudicial end-state and risking a functional return to the catalyst theory. Justice Kagan’s administrability concern reinforces that tying fee eligibility to interim orders in mooted cases would expand “prevailing” beyond the text and our precedent without a principled limiting rule.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: I take the Chief Justice’s and Justice Kagan’s administrability concern seriously: we must avoid fee awards that effectively track voluntary repeal and drift toward Buckhannon’s rejected catalyst theory. But that concern is met by tying “prevailing party” to whether the preliminary injunction itself delivered enforceable, merits-inflected relief that materially altered the parties’ legal relationship while it remained operative—distinct from merely prompting legislative change. Justice Thomas’s and Justice Alito’s emphasis on “enduring” relief at the conclusion reads Sole v. Wyner too broadly; Sole barred fees when an interim win is undone by a merits loss, and it expressly left open the mootness posture where the court’s order is never reversed and provides the real-world protection sought. On a pragmatic, procedural-fairness view of § 1988’s function, a categorical no-fees rule in mooted preliminary-injunction cases would systematically penalize civil-rights plaintiffs who secured meaningful court-ordered relief but were deprived of final judgment by happenstance or strategic mooting.

John Roberts.reasoning: Section 1988(b) authorizes fees only for a "prevailing party," which under Buckhannon requires a judicially sanctioned, enduring material alteration of the parties’ legal relationship, not merely a catalytic effect. A preliminary injunction—entered on a predictive "likelihood of success" standard (Winter) and not culminating in a final merits judgment before mootness—ordinarily lacks the necessary permanence and merits resolution, and Sole v. Wyner cautions that preliminary relief, standing alone, does not establish prevailing-party status absent an enduring merits-based victory. Where the lasting change results from legislative repeal rather than a final court-ordered merits disposition, treating plaintiffs as prevailing would expand § 1988 beyond a narrow, administrable rule and risk fee awards untethered to conclusive judicial relief. A narrow holding denying fees in this posture best preserves the Buckhannon/Sole framework and avoids encouraging fee litigation over provisional orders that never ripen into final adjudications.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: Section 1988(b) authorizes fees only for a "prevailing party," a term of art that, in ordinary legal usage, refers to the party in whose favor a judgment is rendered; a preliminary injunction based on a likelihood-of-success prediction is not a final merits judgment. Under Buckhannon Bd. & Care Home, Inc. v. W. Va. Dep’t of Health & Human Res., prevailing status requires a judicially sanctioned, material alteration of the parties’ legal relationship—one that makes the plaintiff "entitled to enforce a judgment, consent decree, or settlement"—and that did not occur once the case became moot without a conclusive merits resolution. Sole v. Wyner reinforces that interim success does not confer prevailing-party status when it is not followed by enduring relief on the merits. Because any lasting change here resulted from legislative repeal rather than a final, enforceable merits disposition, respondents are not prevailing parties under § 1988.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: Section 1988(b) authorizes fees only for a "prevailing party," which this Court has tied to a judicially sanctioned, material alteration of the parties’ legal relationship that is sufficiently enduring. Under Buckhannon Board & Care Home, Inc. v. West Virginia DHHR, the lasting change must be attributable to judicial action rather than a nonjudicial event like legislative repeal, and awarding fees where mootness intervenes risks resurrecting the rejected catalyst theory. Sole v. Wyner further indicates that success at the preliminary-injunction stage—reflecting only a likelihood-of-success assessment—does not establish prevailing status when the case ends without a merits-resolving judgment and the preliminary relief does not endure through final disposition. Because the only enduring change here flowed from repeal rather than an ultimate judicial determination on the merits, respondents are not prevailing parties under § 1988(b).

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: Section 1988(b) aims to ensure access to justice by enabling civil-rights plaintiffs to obtain counsel when they secure meaningful, court-ordered relief, and an enforceable preliminary injunction that halts enforcement against the plaintiffs can materially alter the parties’ legal relationship with the requisite judicial imprimatur. Buckhannon rejects “catalyst” theories where change comes solely from voluntary defendant action, but here the change was judicially ordered while the injunction was in effect, providing concrete, merits-inflected relief under the Winter likelihood-of-success framework. Sole v. Wyner held that a plaintiff who ultimately loses on the merits cannot claim prevailing-party status based on an “ephemeral” preliminary win, but it expressly left open whether preliminary-injunction success can suffice when there is no adverse final merits determination and the case becomes moot. Where mootness follows and the plaintiffs obtained the practical protection they sought through a court order, treating them as prevailing parties best fits § 1988’s remedial purpose and avoids undermining enforcement of constitutional rights for vulnerable litigants.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: Section 1988(b) authorizes fees only for a "prevailing party," which under Buckhannon requires a judicially sanctioned, material alteration of the parties’ legal relationship—typically through an enforceable judgment or comparable merits-based disposition. A preliminary injunction is ordinarily an interim order issued on a predictive "likelihood of success" standard and, as Sole v. Wyner emphasizes, does not by itself supply the enduring, merits-resolving victory that fee-shifting presupposes when the case later becomes moot. Here, because the litigation ended without a final merits determination and the lasting change resulted from legislative repeal rather than a conclusive court order, treating the plaintiffs as prevailing parties would stretch § 1988 beyond its coherent, administrable bounds and invite fees based on tentative, nonfinal rulings. That said, this leaves room for the narrower possibility—consistent with workability—that an injunction could qualify where it effectively grants all the relief on the merits and is functionally final, but this record sounds in the ordinary, nonfinal preliminary-injunction context.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: Section 1988(b) authorizes fees only for a “prevailing party,” a term of art that traditionally refers to a party “in whose favor a judgment is rendered,” and Buckhannon requires a judicially sanctioned, material alteration of the parties’ legal relationship—not merely a practical victory attributable to events outside the court’s decree. A preliminary injunction is by design provisional and typically rests on a predictive “likelihood of success” assessment (Winter), so where the case becomes moot before any final merits judgment, the injunction does not supply the sort of conclusive, enduring judicial relief that marks a party as having prevailed. Sole v. Wyner reinforces that preliminary relief, standing alone, does not establish prevailing-party status when it is not followed by a merits-resolving judgment; and when the lasting change comes from legislative repeal rather than a final court order, awarding fees would resemble the catalyst theory Buckhannon rejected. Reading “prevailing party” to include any plaintiff who secures interim relief before mootness would expand § 1988 beyond its text and invite fee awards untethered to a final judicial disposition altering legal rights.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: Under 42 U.S.C. § 1988(b), a plaintiff must obtain a judicially sanctioned, material alteration of the parties’ legal relationship—typically through a judgment on the merits or a comparable enduring order. Buckhannon rejects “catalyst” theories and indicates that prevailing-party status generally requires enforceable relief akin to a judgment, consent decree, or settlement, not merely a provisional assessment. Sole v. Wyner further counsels that a preliminary injunction that does not culminate in a final merits resolution is ordinarily insufficient to confer prevailing-party status, especially where the case later becomes moot by legislative repeal rather than an enduring judicial determination. As a practical, workability matter, treating short-lived preliminary injunctions as “prevailing” would invite fee awards based on tentative likelihood-of-success rulings and blur the line Buckhannon drew between judicial relief and non-judicial change.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: Section 1988(b) authorizes fees only for a "prevailing party," a term this Court has tied to a judicially sanctioned, material alteration of the parties’ legal relationship that endures at the conclusion of the litigation. Under Buckhannon Board & Care Home, Inc. v. West Virginia Department of Health & Human Resources, the alteration must be court-ordered rather than the product of nonjudicial events; here, the only enduring change resulted from legislative repeal mooting the suit. And Sole v. Wyner teaches that preliminary injunctive relief that does not culminate in lasting merits relief is not enough, because a preliminary injunction reflects only a likelihood-of-success assessment and is inherently provisional under Winter v. NRDC. Treating such interim relief as “prevailing” when the case ends without a merits judgment would effectively resurrect the catalyst theory Buckhannon rejected.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: Section 1988(b) turns on whether the plaintiff obtained a court-ordered, merits-based change in the parties’ legal relationship, and a preliminary injunction can satisfy that standard when it is an enforceable order that grants the concrete relief sought, not merely a “transient victory at the threshold.” Sole v. Wyner holds only that a preliminary injunction followed by an ultimate loss on the merits does not confer prevailing-party status, but it does not categorically bar fees where the plaintiff’s injunction-based success is never undone and the case becomes moot for reasons unrelated to a merits defeat. Consistent with Buckhannon’s requirement of “judicial imprimatur,” an injunction that halts enforcement against plaintiffs is court-sanctioned relief that materially alters legal obligations while it remains in force, and Lefemine reinforces that obtaining injunctive relief is paradigmatic prevailing-party success. Denying fees categorically here would undercut § 1988’s remedial purpose by discouraging civil-rights plaintiffs—especially those challenging punitive state practices—from seeking prompt, practical relief where procedural fairness and real-world consequences favor recognizing their court-ordered victory.
